title: A second life for car batteries
bodyMd:
An electric car's battery is usually retired long before it has stopped being useful. Manufacturers commonly guarantee that a pack will keep around 70 to 80 per cent of its original capacity for eight years or so; once it falls much below that, the driver notices the shorter range and the pack is replaced. Yet a battery that can no longer carry a car as far as it once did can still store a great deal of electricity, and a stationary store beside a solar farm, a factory or a block of flats does not care how heavy or bulky its battery is.

Giving such packs a "second life" before they are recycled therefore has an obvious appeal. Making the battery is the most energy-hungry part of building an electric car, and every extra year of use spreads that one-off cost over more stored kilowatt-hours. Recycling, by contrast, recovers valuable metals, but it consumes energy of its own and ends whatever useful life the pack had left.

In practice, the second life has proved harder to arrange than the first. Packs come from dozens of car models, each with its own shape, chemistry and control electronics, so a store may have to be designed around whatever happens to be available. Nor is it easy to know what is being bought. Two packs of the same model and age can differ widely in health, depending on how they were charged and in what climate they were driven, and testing each one thoroughly costs time and money. A housing cooperative that built a store from 120 used packs found that within three years it had to remove almost a quarter of them, against the one in twenty it had allowed for.

The economics are shifting as well. Every fall in the price of new storage batteries narrows the gap that second-life packs were meant to exploit: if a new pack, with a full warranty and predictable behaviour, costs only a little more than a used one, many buyers will pay the difference. Second life is therefore likely to survive not as a general answer but where its advantages are greatest, in large batches of identical packs from a single model whose history is known.
